pairs.subject: media-playback
pairs.evidence: crates/shadowrunr-clips/src/render.rs:704 The clip factory is an offline batch encoder. It cuts the recording with ffmpeg, has headless Chromium record the stage, checks the output with ffprobe and writes files to disk. It never plays media against a real-world clock under transport control: no app-owned play/pause/seek, no live engine switching, no continuity. A case-insensitive grep of crates/shadowrunr-clips and crates/shadowrunr-daemon found no hits for crossfade, requestAnimationFrame, AudioContext, revokeObjectURL or underflow.

techniques.evidence: crates/shadowrunr-clips/src/footage.rs:5 The 'clock' here is a fixed offset from stream time into a recorded file, used to choose cut points. It is not a live playhead that consumers sample.
crates/shadowrunr-clips/src/render.rs:5 This crate only serializes scene events on the clip's clock. Scheduling them against a clock happens in apps/stage, which is outside this context.
crates/shadowrunr-clips/src/footage.rs:425 ffmpeg runs as a one-shot batch transcoder. It is not a playback engine behind a transport contract with capabilities.

crates/shadowrunr-clips/src/render.rs:706 This is a single blocking record-then-verify call with no transport verbs or playback state machine. The recorder's .output() has no deadline, but that is a subprocess-lifecycle concern, not a playback-transition watchdog.
